segments.say: Long before brain scanners and smartphones, people were thinking deeply about habits. One of the most famous early writers on the subject was the American psychologist and philosopher William James. In eighteen ninety, he published a huge book called The Principles of Psychology. And one of its chapters was simply called Habit.

James wrote about habits with remarkable insight, and a lovely turn of phrase. He described how our nervous system is shaped by repetition, like paper that has been folded. Once folded, it tends to fall into the same fold again. Each repetition makes the next one easier.

One of his most quoted lines is this. The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy. In other words, rather than fighting ourselves every day, we can train our habits so that they carry us toward the things we value.

show.text: The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy.
show.by: William James, The Principles of Psychology, 1890

segments.say: James also saw how habits free the mind. He wrote that the more of the details of daily life we can hand over to automatic habit, the more our higher powers of mind will be set free for their own proper work. That's very close to what modern research finds. Habits free our attention for what truly matters.

James believed that habits shape character. He imagined people as walking bundles of habits, and warned that, by the time we're adults, many of our habits have set like plaster. That sounds a little harsh. But he wasn't saying change is impossible. He was saying that habits are powerful, and that we should build good ones early and carefully.

And James offered practical advice that still sounds fresh today. When starting a new habit, launch yourself with as strong and decided an initiative as possible. Never suffer an exception to occur till the new habit is securely rooted. And seize the very first possible opportunity to act on every resolution you make.

Modern research has softened some of this advice. Remember Lally's study, where missing a single day didn't ruin habit formation. So we don't need to be quite as strict as James suggested. But his core idea, that repetition shapes us, and that early momentum helps, has held up remarkably well.

What I love about James is how much he understood, without any of today's tools. He watched people carefully, thought deeply, and described patterns that neuroscientists would later find in the brain. The folds in the paper, the chunks in the maze, the ally in the nervous system. Old wisdom and new science, telling the same story.

So as we explore habits tonight, I'd like to keep James's beautiful phrase in mind. Make your nervous system your ally. Not by fighting it, but by gently training it. By repeating what you'd like to become, until it becomes the easiest thing to do.

So here's what William James teaches us. He wrote about habit more than a century ago, with insights that still ring true. Repetition shapes us, like paper that falls into the same fold. Habits free our minds for higher things. And the great task is to make our nervous system our ally, instead of our enemy.

segments.say: So how much of what we do each day is actually habit? You might be surprised. Modern researchers have tried to measure it, by asking people to note what they were doing, and thinking, throughout the day.
